name: request-batch
context: A client needs several independent operations from the same provider — read a user, list their files, fetch their permissions — and issues them one at a time. Each individual call is cheap, but the chatty sequence dominates the cost: connection setup, TLS handshakes, per-request serialization, and N round trips of network latency that no amount of backend optimization can remove. Request batching (also catalogued as Request Bundle, Request Deck, or Bulk Request-Response) defines a single request message that carries many independent sub-requests, each with its own id, method, URL, headers, and optional body; the provider unpacks the bundle, executes the sub-requests, and returns a response bundle whose entries mirror the request structure, correlated by the same ids. The semantics are deliberately weak: a sub-request that fails does not roll back its siblings, which is exactly why the pattern only applies to genuinely independent operations. Microsoft Graph caps a JSON batch at 20 requests and exposes dependsOn for the cases that are not independent; Facebook Graph caps at 50 and counts every call inside a batch against the same rate limits, so batching reduces round trips without buying extra quota. A client may also assemble the bundle itself, with a time-window threshold that collects queries issued within 50ms into one dispatch — which is how most real implementations decide what goes in a batch.
benefits: N network round trips collapse into one, so latency for a screen of independent reads drops from the sum of N calls to roughly one call
Connection reuse and header amortization: TLS handshake, TCP setup, and authentication are paid once per bundle instead of per sub-request
Serialization and parsing overhead is amortized — one envelope is parsed rather than N separate documents

Per-sub-request failure isolation becomes explicit and safe: one failed operation returns its own status in the response bundle without affecting siblings, unlike a single all-or-nothing composite call
Each sub-request can still carry its own method, URL, headers, and body, so the batch is heterogeneous and does not force a new bespoke bulk endpoint per use case
Response entries are correlatable by id even when the provider returns them out of order, so the client can match results without relying on position
Side effect on the client's cache and telemetry: batching reduces total requests, which improves the effect of any request rate limit on a well-behaved client
Deprioritization is possible without changing semantics — long-running sub-requests (report generation, export) can be split into their own asynchronous bundle
tradeoffs: Head-of-line blocking: a batched response is only as fast as its slowest sub-request, so one slow operation delays every unrelated operation sharing the bundle
Retries are much coarser — a network failure loses the whole bundle, so the client must be able to re-issue sub-requests idempotently or accept partial completion
Debugging gets materially harder: network tooling shows one request instead of many, and per-operation latency is no longer visible in the browser's request list
Whole-query caching degrades — a bundled operation's effective TTL is the shortest TTL of any field it contains, so adding fields makes the entire bundle less cacheable
Error semantics must be designed explicitly; a 200 on the bundle does not mean the sub-requests succeeded, and clients that check only the outer status will silently swallow failures
Batch size caps and per-sub-request rate limits still apply, so batching reduces chatter without granting additional quota — providers still count each sub-request
Payload growth increases memory pressure on both ends, and very large bundles can exceed request-size limits or URL-length constraints
Adds a client-side buffer and a dispatch window, which introduces its own latency and can batch requests that were never logically related
use_cases: A dashboard assembling 8 independent widgets, each fetching from the same API, into one dispatch on page load
A mobile client on a high-latency link batching profile, notification-count, and settings reads to avoid three radio round trips
A data sync job issuing thousands of independent per-record reads or writes through a bulk endpoint instead of one HTTP call each
Microsoft Graph's $batch JSON endpoint, where up to 20 independent requests travel in one POST and each response carries its own status
GraphQL clients collecting colocated component queries issued within a dispatch window into a single array-of-operations request
Bypassing URL-length limits by moving complex filter expressions from the query string into the request body of a batched call
avoid_when: The sub-requests are dependent — later operations need earlier results, which is what dependsOn is for, and full dependency graphs belong in an orchestration pattern
One slow sub-request would hold back fast, user-visible results; debatch or split the slow operations out instead
You have not fixed the underlying over-fetching — batching five redundant queries into one request still executes five queries
The provider has no per-sub-request status semantics, so a client cannot tell which operation failed and the whole bundle must be retried
Operations are not idempotent and a mid-bundle network failure would duplicate side effects on replay
The interaction is a single dependent read-modify-write, where a composite all-or-nothing endpoint is the correct mechanism, not a bundle
component_types: Request Bundle: the container format holding an array of independent sub-requests, each with an id, method, relative URL, headers, and optional body
Batch Endpoint: the provider route that accepts a bundle — Graph $batch, a multipart/mixed endpoint, or an array-of-operations body
Metadata Element: correlation ids that let the response bundle be matched back to request entries even out of order
Bundle Dispatcher: the client-side buffer with a time or size threshold that collects candidate operations before sending
Response Bundle: the mirrored structure of per-sub-request status, headers, and body, plus a bundle-level envelope status
Idempotency Key: the per-operation token that makes safe replay of a partially failed bundle possible
Dependency Descriptor: the dependsOn or sequencing metadata that expresses the rare cases where bundled operations are ordered
anti_patterns: Batching enabled by default at project start with no measured evidence that request count is the actual problem
A generalized tunnel endpoint that accepts arbitrary unrelated operations, which hides API semantics behind a transport trick and is explicitly advised against in REST cookbook guidance
Checking only the outer 200 status and discarding per-sub-request statuses, silently losing failed operations
Combining every query on a page into one giant bundle, destroying whole-operation cache hit rates for all of them
Retrying an entire non-idempotent bundle after a transport failure, duplicating side effects
Batching fast user-blocking reads together with slow reporting calls so the whole screen waits on the report
Assuming batching buys quota — providers still count every sub-request against rate limits and still enforce a bundle size cap
design_principles: Bundle only independent work: the safety of the pattern rests entirely on the absence of dependencies between sub-requests
Per-sub-request semantics over bundle semantics: every entry carries its own status, and the bundle-level status says nothing about whether the operations succeeded
Correlation by identity, never by position — assign explicit ids and match responses by id, since providers may return entries out of order
Idempotent replay: the design must tolerate a whole-bundle retry, because transport failures do not respect partial success
Batching is a transport optimization, not an API redesign — it must not change what any individual operation means or what it is authorized to do
Fix over-fetching first — reducing the number of operations needed is a better fix than packing them together more efficiently
Isolate the slow: expected-latency differences between operations are a reason to split the bundle, not to merge it
best_practices: Establish a measured baseline first — count actual round trips per user action before introducing batching
Try cheaper fixes in order: automatic persisted queries, CDN caching, partial query caching, then HTTP/2 multiplexing, before reaching for batching
Give every sub-request a unique id and validate uniqueness client-side, since providers reject the whole bundle on a duplicate
Cap bundle size at the provider's documented maximum and chunk above it, with per-chunk retry
Propagate per-sub-request status into client error handling and telemetry so failures remain attributable
Attach idempotency keys to mutating sub-requests so a bundle retry is safe
Add a debatch escape hatch for operations known to be slow, and drive it from observed latency rather than from a static list
